Monkwearmouth
munk-WEER-mowth
n. (the monastery at the mouth of the Wear, founded by Benedict Biscop in 674, the elder of the twin houses with Jarrow)
Old English Æt Wiramuthan, at the mouth of the Wear, with monk prefixed to distinguish the monastic settlement from the town.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Monkwearmouth, the house at the mouth of the Wear, was founded in 674 when Ecgfrith gave Benedict Biscop seventy hides of land, and it was the elder of the twin monasteries that were always governed as one. Biscop built it of stone in the Roman manner and sent to Gaul for glaziers, so that glass windows returned to England after two centuries; he brought masons, service books, pictures for the walls, and the chief cantor of St Peter's at Rome to teach the house to sing. Bede entered it as a boy of seven under Abbot Benedict before being moved to Jarrow, and he wrote the lives of its abbots. The two houses together held some six hundred monks at their height. Danish raids and the Conquest ruined it, and the Norman priory that followed was a cell of Durham. The dictionary records Monkwearmouth because it shows what a founder is for: Biscop himself wrote no book and is remembered for no sermon, yet every stone, window, song and volume that made Bede possible was fetched by him. The foundation is not the building; but someone has to lay it, and the men who lay foundations are rarely the men whose names the work carries.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a foundation as the basis of an edifice; a corner stone as the stone which unites two walls; to build as to construct and raise; a mind as intention or disposition; and a wall as a work of stone or brick for defence or enclosure.

expand to see more

FOUNDATION, n. The basis of an edifice; that part of a building which lies on the ground; the act of fixing the basis; the basis or ground work of any thing.

CORNER STONE, n. The stone which lies at the corner of two walls, and unites them; the principal stone, and especially the stone which forms the corner of the foundation.

BUILD, v.t. To frame, construct and raise, as an edifice or fabric of almost any kind.

MIND, n. Intention; purpose; design; inclination; will; desire.

WALL, n. A work or structure of stone, brick or other materials, raised to some height, and intended for a defence or security.

Key Scripture

1Co 3:11 — "For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ."

Eph 2:20 — "And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone;"

Psa 127:1 — "A Song of degrees for Solomon. Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain."

Neh 4:6 — "So built we the wall; and all the wall was joined together unto the half thereof: for the people had a mind to work."

Modern Corruption

The elder of the twin Northumbrian houses, founded 674 by Benedict Biscop, who fetched the books, glass, masons and song that made Bede's Jarrow possible.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that founders are servants of a foundation they did not lay. Paul will allow no rival to that one basis, “For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1Co 3:11), and the household he describes is built on apostolic teaching with “Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone” (Eph 2:20). Biscop's stone and glass were worth fetching only because that foundation was already laid.

The live temptation runs the other way, toward trusting the apparatus. Monkwearmouth had the best masonry, the best choir and the best library in England, and the Psalter has the answer to any confidence placed in such things: “Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it” (Psa 127:1). What makes a building project succeed under God is a willing people rather than a grand plan, which is exactly how Nehemiah accounts for his wall: “for the people had a mind to work” (Neh 4:6). Biscop's six hundred monks had that mind, and one boy among them wrote the history of the English church.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek themelios (G2310), a foundation; Greek akrogoniaios (G0204), chief corner stone; Hebrew banah (H1129), to build; Hebrew leb (H3820), heart or mind.

expand to see more

Greek themelios (G2310) — a foundation, the basis of a building; “For other foundation can no man lay”, 1 Corinthians 3:11.

Greek akrogoniaios (G0204) — the chief corner stone; “Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone”, Ephesians 2:20.

Hebrew banah (H1129) — to build, to establish; “Except the LORD build the house”, Psalm 127:1.

Hebrew amal (H5998) — to toil, to labour; “they labour in vain that build it”, Psalm 127:1.

Hebrew leb (H3820) — the heart, the mind, the will; “for the people had a mind to work”, Nehemiah 4:6.

Usage

"“For other foundation can no man lay” (1Co 3:11) — what no founder supplies."

"“Except the LORD build the house” (Psa 127:1) — said over the best masonry in England."

"“for the people had a mind to work” (Neh 4:6) — six hundred monks in two houses."
